Kevin Trudeau says a vitamin on your label isn't always the vitamin it claims to be.

His example: real niacin can cause a short 'niacin flush' - your skin turning warm and red for a few minutes while it works. Some people didn't like that feeling, so a chemist created niacinamide, a different compound that skips the flush entirely.

The catch, in Kevin's words: niacinamide isn't niacin. But plenty of labels still print 'niacin' in bold, with 'as niacinamide' tucked into parentheses right after it.

His advice: read past the big word on the front. If the parentheses say niacinamide, you're not getting the niacin your brain is asking for.

#kevintrudeau #wbdaily #niacin #readthelabel #supplementfacts #healthtruth

Kevin Trudeau says real vitamin E isn't one single ingredient - it's a family.

His example: years ago, scientists made a lab version of vitamin E called D-alpha-tocopherol and sold it as the real thing. Later, researchers who studied whole foods like walnuts found that natural vitamin E is actually made of four different tocopherols, working together.

Kevin's point: a single synthetic tocopherol isn't the same as what nature packs into a walnut or a seed.

Next time you pick up a vitamin E bottle, look for 'mixed tocopherols' on the label, not just one name.
